title: 6 Best Concrete Sealers in 2026: One Pick for Each Slab
metaDescription: Foundation Armor SX5000 WB is the best concrete sealer for most outdoor slabs; 6 picks cover driveways, steps, patios, garage floors and basements.
keywords: best concrete sealer for sidewalks and carports
review of film forming concrete sealers
intro:
The best concrete sealer for most homes is Foundation Armor SX5000 WB, a water-based silane-siloxane that soaks in, leaves no film and keeps outdoor concrete looking exactly as it does now. It is the least risky choice for walks, steps, patios and driveways.

The catch is that one can rarely suits every slab in the house. A salted driveway, a patio you want to look richer, an oil-spotted garage floor and a damp basement each fail in a different way, so this guide gives each one its own pick and explains how to tell which family of sealer the job needs.
quickAnswer: Buy Foundation Armor SX5000 WB for outdoor concrete you want protected but unchanged. Step up to Ghostshield Siloxa-Tek 8500 for driveways and walks that get salted every winter. Use Foundation Armor AR350 for a wet look on a patio, Rust-Oleum EpoxyShield for a garage floor, RadonSeal Plus for bare basement concrete, and Seal-Krete Clear-Seal for a small covered porch on a budget.

sections.heading: Best Concrete Sealer: The Short Answer
sections.body:
| Pick | Best for | Key spec |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Foundation Armor SX5000 WB | Most outdoor concrete | Water-based silane-siloxane, no film |
| Ghostshield Siloxa-Tek 8500 | Salted driveways, walks and steps | Concentrated silane-siloxane |
| Foundation Armor AR350 | Patios that should look wet | Solvent acrylic, low-gloss film |
| Rust-Oleum EpoxyShield | Garage floors | Two-part water-based epoxy kit |
| RadonSeal Plus | Basement floors and walls | Reactive silicate penetrant |
| Seal-Krete Clear-Seal | Small covered porches and steps | Budget acrylic, gloss or satin |

There is no single best concrete sealer, because there is no single kind of concrete problem. Outdoors in snow country, the enemy is salty water that soaks in and freezes. On a patio, it is usually looks. In the garage it is oil, and in the basement it is moisture rising from below.

That is why the top two picks are penetrating repellents: they cover the most common job, exterior concrete, without changing the surface or leaving anything to peel. The other four are matched to the slabs a repellent cannot handle. If your only concern is the driveway, our [concrete driveway sealer rankings](/best-concrete-driveway-sealer-reviews/) go deeper on that one surface.

sections.heading: The 6 Best Concrete Sealers in 2026, Ranked
sections.body:
The order below reflects how many homes each product suits and how hard it is to get wrong. Picks are based on manufacturer data sheets, labeled coverage, published service-life ranges and recurring owner feedback, not hands-on lab work. Where a claim comes from the maker, it is stated that way.

### Best Overall: Foundation Armor SX5000 WB

SX5000 WB is the sealer to buy when you want a slab protected without looking any different. It is a water-carried blend of silane and siloxane that travels into the pores and reacts there, leaving the pore walls water-repellent instead of building a coat on top. With no film, there is nothing to scuff in traffic lanes, yellow in sun or peel when moisture rises from the soil. Foundation Armor lists it for driveways, sidewalks, pool decks, pavers, brick and block, and the water carrier keeps the smell mild enough for a walkout basement patio or an open garage. The downside is that you cannot see it once it dries, so missed strips are easy; work in marked sections with a pump sprayer. It is a water and salt repellent first, so oil drips still need prompt cleanup.

**Pros:** No sheen, color change or film; low-odor water-based carrier; breathable, so it will not trap moisture; maker cites DOT-style performance criteria; works on concrete and masonry alike.

**Cons:** Invisible when dry, so coverage is hard to track; modest protection against oil; will not give a wet or glossy look.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Foundation+Armor+SX5000+WB&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best for Salted Concrete: Ghostshield Siloxa-Tek 8500

If your driveway, front walk or concrete steps get salted every winter, Siloxa-Tek 8500 is the step up. Ghostshield built the line around chloride exposure, the slow process where salty meltwater soaks into the top layer, freezes and pops off thin flakes known as scaling. It ships as a concentrate you dilute with water, so the jug price looks high while the cost per square foot works out reasonable. Like SX5000, it leaves no film, keeps the broom texture and grip, and gives shovels and plow blades nothing to chip. Follow the dilution printed on the current label exactly instead of a number from a forum, since ratios can change between formulations. On a sheltered patio in a dry climate it is more product than the job needs.

**Pros:** Formulated with road salt in mind; concentrate lowers cost per square foot; no change in color or texture; breathable; suited to big exterior areas.

**Cons:** Dilution must be measured carefully; overkill for mild climates; higher upfront spend.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Ghostshield+Siloxa-Tek+8500&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best for Patios: Foundation Armor AR350

AR350 is for people who want the patio to look freshly hosed down all the time. It is a solvent-carried acrylic that forms a thin film, deepening the color of gray concrete and making exposed aggregate, stamped or tinted slabs stand out. Foundation Armor describes it as a lower-gloss wet look, which suits most backyards better than a mirror finish. A useful trait of solvent acrylics is that a fresh coat partly softens the one below, so touch-ups blend in and mild whitening can often be cleared with solvent instead of stripping. The film is also its weakness: it wears in traffic paths, it needs recoating every few years, and it turns slick when wet unless you stir in an anti-slip grit. Solvent odor means outdoor use only, and some states restrict high-VOC versions.

**Pros:** Rich wet look without high gloss; recoats bond well; popular for stamped and aggregate concrete; quick dry in good weather.

**Cons:** Strong solvent smell; film wears and needs recoats; slippery when wet without grit.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Foundation+Armor+AR350&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best for Garage Floors: Rust-Oleum EpoxyShield

A garage floor is the one slab where a water repellent is the wrong answer. Water is rarely the issue there; motor oil, transmission fluid and salty slush are. EpoxyShield is a two-part water-based epoxy kit that cures into a hard, continuous coat, so spills sit on top and wipe off instead of wicking into the concrete. The kit includes a cleaning and etching packet and decorative flakes, and Rust-Oleum labels the standard size for about one car bay. Owner feedback is consistent about the weak points: the cured film is thinner than a professional system, and adhesion depends almost entirely on prep. Do a plastic-sheet moisture test first, and keep it inside the garage door line, because epoxy yellows in sunlight. Our full [Rust-Oleum EpoxyShield review](/rust-oleum-epoxyshield-review/) covers what owners report.

**Pros:** Keeps oil and fluids from soaking in; kit includes cleaner and flakes; sold at most home centers; low odor for an epoxy; easy to clean.

**Cons:** Thin film compared with pro systems; prep decides whether it lasts; not UV stable and not for outdoor slabs.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Rust-Oleum+EpoxyShield+Garage+Floor+Coating&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best for Basements: RadonSeal Plus

Basement concrete gets moisture from the ground side, which is exactly what makes film sealers blister and peel there. RadonSeal Plus is a silicate-based penetrant that soaks deep into bare concrete and reacts with the free lime inside, forming crystals that tighten the pore structure from within. The company markets it for reducing dampness, efflorescence and radon entry and describes the treatment as permanent, since nothing on the surface can wear away. It has limits. A crack that leaks during storms needs injection repair, and water pouring in at the wall-floor joint is a drainage problem. It also needs truly bare concrete, so paint or old sealer must come off first. Once cured, the slab can take paint or flooring, which makes it a sensible step before carpet or vinyl.

**Pros:** Reacts inside the concrete; maker calls it permanent; cuts dampness and efflorescence; water-based for indoor use; leaves the slab ready for flooring.

**Cons:** Will not stop active leaks; needs clean, uncoated concrete; no visible change to judge coverage.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=RadonSeal+Plus+Penetrating+Concrete+Sealer&tag=sktiger-20)

### Best Budget Pick: Seal-Krete Clear-Seal

Some jobs do not justify a specialty order. Clear-Seal is the acrylic you can buy on a Saturday at a home center, roll onto a front step or a covered porch slab, and finish before dinner. It forms a light film in gloss or satin that adds a mild sheen and some color depth, and it resists water spotting and dirt for a while. The film is thinner than premium solvent acrylics, so it dulls faster in sun and foot traffic, and owners commonly report recoating about every two years. On a salted driveway it is the wrong tool; a penetrating repellent will outlast it several times over. It makes sense on small, sheltered surfaces where you want some shine and do not mind a quick redo now and then.

**Pros:** Stocked at most home centers; low upfront cost; gloss and satin options; easy to roll or spray; mild color boost.

**Cons:** Shorter service life; needs frequent recoats outdoors; poor choice for salted slabs.

[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Seal-Krete+Clear-Seal&tag=sktiger-20)

sections.heading: Which Concrete Sealer Do You Need for Each Slab?
sections.body:
Name the threat first, then pick the chemistry. Most bad experiences with concrete sealer come from buying one product and spreading it across surfaces that fail for different reasons.

| Slab | Main threat | Sealer family | Pick |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Driveway, sidewalk, carport | Water, salt, freeze-thaw | Silane-siloxane penetrating | Siloxa-Tek 8500 or SX5000 WB |
| Steps and stoops | Salt, foot traffic, slipping | Silane-siloxane penetrating | Siloxa-Tek 8500 |
| Open patio | Water, sun, looks | Penetrating or acrylic film | SX5000 WB or AR350 |
| Garage floor | Oil, fluids, hot tires | Epoxy or polyaspartic coating | EpoxyShield |
| Basement floor or wall | Moisture from below | Reactive silicate | RadonSeal Plus |
| Small covered porch | Dirt, light wear | Budget acrylic | Clear-Seal |

### Driveways, sidewalks, carports and steps

Use a penetrating repellent. It leaves the surface texture alone, so steps and sloped walks keep their grip, and it keeps salty water out of the top layer where scaling starts. Stamped or colored driveways are the exception; see the [stamped concrete sealer](/best-stamped-concrete-sealer/) picks for those.

### Patios and pool surrounds

Decide whether you like how the slab looks dry. If you do, a penetrating sealer protects it invisibly. If you want deeper color, only a film sealer gives it, and you accept recoats every few years.

### Garage floors and workshops

Use a coating, not a repellent. Oil and brake fluid pass through water repellents, so the drip spot under the engine becomes permanent. Our [garage floor coating guide](/best-garage-floor-coating/) compares epoxy, polycuramine and polyaspartic options.

### Basements and slabs headed under flooring

Use a silicate that tightens the concrete from inside and stays breathable. Avoid silicone-based repellents under carpet, tile or vinyl adhesive, because they can stop the next product from bonding.

sections.heading: Penetrating vs Film-Forming Concrete Sealers: What Is the Difference?
sections.body:
Penetrating sealers protect the concrete; film sealers protect the look. Keep that rule in mind and the rest of the label makes sense.

### Silane and siloxane repellents

These are small silicon-based molecules carried in water or solvent. They soak into the pores, react with moisture and the alkaline cement, and leave the pore walls water-repellent. Silane is the smaller molecule and reaches deeper into dense concrete; siloxane is larger and suits porous masonry. Most retail products blend the two, which is explained in our [silane vs siloxane guide](/silane-vs-siloxane-sealers/). Labels and makers commonly rate them for 5 to 10 years outdoors.

### Silicate densifiers

Sodium, potassium and lithium silicates react with free lime to form extra binder inside the surface. They harden the top layer, cut dusting and tighten pores, but on their own they repel water only modestly. They are common indoors and as a first step on old, sandy outdoor slabs before a repellent.

### Acrylics

Acrylics are the most common film sealers. Solvent-based versions darken and enrich the most; water-based versions smell less and usually look a little flatter. The film is what you see and what wears, typically lasting 2 to 4 years outdoors.

### Polyurethanes and epoxies

These are tougher films. Polyurethane often goes on as a topcoat where abrasion and chemicals matter. Epoxy is the hardest common option, which is why it owns the garage, but it yellows in sunlight and can lift from slabs with moisture coming through. Neither belongs on a typical driveway.

### Reading film-forming sealer reviews

When owners complain about a film sealer, the story is usually peeling, whitening or slipperiness, and almost all of it traces back to damp concrete, thick coats or a film used where a repellent belonged. Complaints about penetrating sealers tend to be about not seeing any change, which is the point of them.

sections.heading: Is It Necessary to Seal a Concrete Walkway or Driveway?
sections.body:
Usually yes in a climate with hard freezes and road salt, and often optional in a mild, dry one. A two-minute water test tells you more than the age of the slab.

### Run the water drop test

Sprinkle a cup of water on a clean, dry patch and watch for five minutes. If the concrete darkens quickly and the water vanishes, the surface is absorbent and a sealer will make a real difference. If the water beads and sits, an old sealer is still working or the surface is too dense for a penetrating product to enter right now.

### Climate matters more than age

The damage mechanism outdoors is water entering the top layer, freezing, expanding and flaking off the surface. Where that happens dozens of times a winter, sealing pays off quickly. In places with little frost, an unsealed broom-finished walk can go decades with only cosmetic stains. Sealing still keeps it cleaner, but the return is smaller.

### Is sealing worth the cost?

Compare it to the repair. Once a walk or driveway starts scaling, no product restores the lost surface, and resurfacing or replacement costs far more than a pail of repellent every several years. For a full breakdown of what homeowners and contractors spend, see [how much it costs to seal a driveway](/how-much-does-it-cost-to-seal-a-driveway/).

### When not to seal

Slabs with active structural cracks, heaving or settling need repair first, because sealer will not hold concrete together. A slab with an intact film sealer should not get a penetrating product on top, since the repellent cannot reach the concrete through the film. And a basement floor that sweats should never get a non-breathable coating before the moisture source is handled.

sections.heading: How Do You Seal New Concrete, Old Concrete and Previously Sealed Concrete?
sections.body:
The age and history of the slab decide the prep, and sometimes the product.

### New concrete

Most film sealers ask you to wait about 28 days so excess water can leave and the surface can gain strength. Sealing a green slab with acrylic traps that moisture and is a classic cause of a cloudy, white finish. Some silane-siloxane and cure-and-seal products are labeled for earlier use, sometimes within days, but only follow that if the label you are holding says so.

The first winter is the riskiest time for a new walk or driveway. If it was poured in late summer or fall, getting a penetrating repellent on before the first snow matters more than any later treatment. Avoid deicers on concrete under a year old where you can; our [ice melt for concrete guide](/best-ice-melt-for-concrete/) covers gentler options.

### Old concrete

Old concrete is mostly a cleaning job. Dirt, mildew, tire marks and oil all block a sealer from soaking in. Pressure washing with a surface cleaner, plus a degreaser on stains, is usually enough. Treat deep oil spots before sealing, because a sealer locks in whatever is there; [how to get oil out of concrete](/how-to-get-oil-out-of-concrete/) walks through what works. On a dusty, sandy surface, a silicate densifier first and a repellent second handles both problems.

### Previously sealed concrete

Match the chemistry or remove the old coat. Solvent acrylic goes over solvent acrylic, and water-based acrylic generally goes over water-based acrylic after cleaning. Switching from a film to a penetrating sealer means stripping the film completely. Going from a repellent to a film is usually possible once the repellent has weathered enough that water soaks in again; check with a water test and a small tape-adhesion patch first.

sections.heading: Which Concrete Sealer Finish Is Safest on Steps and Walkways?
sections.body:
A penetrating sealer is the safest choice for steps, ramps, pool decks and sloped walks, because it leaves the original texture alone. A broom-finished step stays exactly as grippy as it was before sealing.

### Why film sealers get slippery

Every film adds some smoothness, and that smoothness turns into slipperiness when the surface is wet, frosty or covered in pool water. High-gloss wet-look products are the worst. Satin films are a little better but still slicker than bare concrete.

### Adding traction to an acrylic

If you want an acrylic look on a walking surface, plan for grip. The usual fix is an anti-slip additive, a fine polymer grit stirred into the final coat. It barely changes the look but noticeably changes the feel underfoot. Keep stirring while you work, or the grit settles in the bucket and the first half of the job gets all of it.

### Color without a film

Some penetrating sealers come in an enhancing version that darkens concrete slightly without forming a film. That is a good middle path on stained or tinted steps that look washed out but must stay grippy.

### Test a patch first

Seal a small, out-of-the-way spot and let it dry for a day. Check the color in sunlight, walk on it in shoes and bare feet, then wet it with a hose. Ten minutes of testing prevents the most common regret: a patio that looks great in photos and feels like ice after rain.

sections.heading: How Much Concrete Sealer Do You Need?
sections.body:
Measure the area, use the label coverage for your surface, and add 10 to 15 percent for waste and thirsty spots.

### Typical coverage

Coverage depends on how porous the concrete is, so labels give a range. A broom-finished exterior slab commonly takes penetrating sealer at about 100 to 200 square feet per gallon per coat. Dense, troweled garage floors absorb less; old, weathered concrete absorbs more. Acrylic labels usually list roughly 150 to 300 square feet per gallon for the first coat, with the second going further because the first has filled the pores.

### A worked example

A two-car driveway of 20 by 40 feet is 800 square feet. At 150 square feet per gallon, two coats need about 11 gallons once you add a little extra. That is two 5-gallon pails with some left for the front walk. Penetrating products often go on wet-on-wet, which uses slightly more than two separate coats would.

### Cost per year beats price per pail

Compare products by how long they last, not just what the pail costs. A premium repellent rated for seven or more years can be cheaper over a decade than a budget acrylic redone every two years, even if the pail costs twice as much. On a tiny area, where your time matters more than material, a quick acrylic recoat can still make sense.

### Hiring it out

Contractor pricing varies widely by region and by whether cleaning and crack repair are included. Ask for a written quote that names the product, the number of coats and the coverage rate. A bid that does not name the product cannot be compared with any other.

sections.heading: How Do You Apply Concrete Sealer?
sections.body:
The steps differ a little by product, but the order never changes: clean, repair, dry, check the weather, then apply thin, even coats. Most failures come from skipping one of those, not from the sealer.

### Clean and repair

Pressure wash, degrease stains and rinse well. Fill cracks with a flexible concrete crack sealant and patch spalled spots so water cannot get under the edges. On a driveway, the full sequence is laid out in [how to seal a concrete driveway](/how-to-seal-a-concrete-driveway/).

### Let it dry completely

Dryness is the step people rush. After washing, give exterior concrete at least 24 hours of dry weather, longer in shade or cool temperatures. Tape a square of plastic to the slab for a few hours; if the underside fogs or the concrete darkens, it is still wet. Sealing damp concrete is the leading cause of a milky acrylic finish.

### Watch the weather

Most labels want air and surface temperatures roughly between 50 and 90 degrees Fahrenheit, no rain for 12 to 24 hours, and no direct midday sun on a hot slab for film formers, which can bubble if the solvent flashes off too fast. Morning or late afternoon in mild weather is ideal.

### Use the right tools

Penetrating sealers go on best with a low-pressure pump sprayer, then a roller or broom to work out puddles. Acrylics go on with a sprayer or short-nap roller in thin coats; thick coats trap solvent and turn cloudy. Solvent products need a sprayer with solvent-rated seals, or the seals swell and leak within minutes.

sections.heading: How Long Does Concrete Sealer Last?
sections.body:
Penetrating silane-siloxane sealers are commonly rated for about 5 to 10 years outdoors, acrylic films for about 2 to 4 years, and silicate densifiers do not wear off the way a film does.

### What shortens it

Traffic, sun and salt. The busiest part of the driveway, the tire turning area and the bottom step lose protection first. Full sun breaks down acrylic films faster, and heavy salting wears repellents toward the low end of their range.

### How to tell it is time

Do a water test on the busiest area rather than going by the calendar. On a penetrating-sealed surface, water that soaks in and darkens the slab within a minute or two means the protection is worn. On an acrylic, look for dull traffic lanes, flaking edges and water that no longer beads.

### Recoat light, not heavy

Recoating an acrylic is easier than the first coat if you stay with the same chemistry: clean, dry and apply one thin coat. Piling on two thick coats every year builds a heavy film that eventually clouds, peels or gets slippery. Less product, applied less often, works better.

### Keep a record

Write down the product name, the date and how much you used. When it is time to reseal, you will know what is on the slab and whether the next product is compatible. That note prevents the most expensive mistake on this page: stripping a slab because nobody remembers what was on it.

mistakes.title: Using one sealer for every slab
mistakes.body: A salted driveway, an oil-stained garage and a damp basement fail for different reasons. A water repellent will not stop oil, and an epoxy will lift off a basement floor with rising moisture. Match the product to the threat on each surface, even if the house ends up with two or three different sealers.

mistakes.title: Sealing concrete that is still damp
mistakes.body: Moisture trapped under an acrylic turns it white and cloudy, and wet pores keep penetrating sealers from soaking in. Give the slab a full dry day after washing, longer in shade or cool weather, and use a taped plastic sheet test whenever you are unsure.

mistakes.title: Laying film sealers on thick
mistakes.body: Heavy coats of acrylic trap solvent, blush white, stay soft and turn slippery. Two thin coats beat one heavy one every time. With penetrating sealers, puddles left to dry can leave a shiny residue, so roll or broom them out before they set.

mistakes.title: Mixing incompatible chemistries
mistakes.body: A water-based acrylic over a solvent acrylic, or a repellent sprayed over an intact film, will not bond or soak in properly. Find out what is already on the slab. If you cannot, test a small patch and check adhesion with tape before committing the whole surface.

mistakes.title: Ignoring traction on steps and walks
mistakes.body: Glossy films on steps, pool decks and sloped walks get slick when wet or frosty. Stir anti-slip grit into the final coat, or choose a penetrating sealer that leaves the original texture alone. A rich wet look is not worth a fall on the front steps.

faqs.q: What is the best concrete sealer?
faqs.a: For most outdoor concrete, a water-based silane-siloxane penetrating sealer such as Foundation Armor SX5000 WB is the best choice. It leaves no film, does not peel or yellow and suits driveways, walks and patios. For heavily salted surfaces, Ghostshield Siloxa-Tek 8500 is the stronger pick. Garage floors need an epoxy coating, and basements need a silicate penetrant instead.

faqs.q: What is the top rated concrete sealer for steps?
faqs.a: A penetrating silane-siloxane such as Ghostshield Siloxa-Tek 8500 is the safest choice for concrete steps. It keeps salty water out of the surface without adding a film, so the steps keep their original grip in rain and frost. If you prefer a sheen, use an acrylic with an anti-slip additive in the final coat.

faqs.q: Can I use the same sealer on my driveway and garage floor?
faqs.a: You can, but one of them will be shortchanged. A penetrating repellent is ideal outside and weak against oil in the garage. An epoxy coating is ideal in the garage and poor outdoors, where sunlight yellows it and freeze-thaw can lift it. Most homes are best served by two products, one for each surface.

faqs.q: What is the best sealer for old concrete?
faqs.a: Clean old concrete thoroughly, then use a penetrating sealer. If the surface is dusty or sandy, apply a silicate densifier first to harden it and follow with a silane-siloxane repellent to keep water and salt out. Fill cracks before sealing, and check with a water test that no old sealer is blocking absorption.

faqs.q: What is the best product to seal a concrete slab before carpet?
faqs.a: A reactive silicate penetrant such as RadonSeal Plus is a good choice before carpet or other flooring. It tightens the concrete from inside, reduces dampness and dusting, and leaves the surface able to accept flooring adhesives once cured. Avoid silicone-based water repellents under flooring, since they can stop adhesives from bonding.

faqs.q: How long should I wait to seal new concrete?
faqs.a: About 28 days for most film-forming sealers, so the slab can release moisture and gain strength. Some penetrating and cure-and-seal products allow earlier use, but only when their label says so. If a slab is poured in fall, try to get a penetrating sealer on before the first freeze and the first round of salt.

faqs.q: Will sealing concrete stop it from cracking?
faqs.a: No. Cracks come from shrinkage, settling, roots, heavy loads and frost movement in the base. A sealer reduces surface damage such as scaling and spalling by keeping water out of the top layer, which can slow the growth of small cracks. Fill existing cracks with a flexible sealant before you seal the slab.

bottomLine: The best concrete sealer is the one matched to the slab in front of you. For outdoor concrete that should look the same and last longer, buy Foundation Armor SX5000 WB, or Ghostshield Siloxa-Tek 8500 where salt is heavy. Use AR350 when a patio should look richer, EpoxyShield on the garage floor, RadonSeal Plus in the basement, and Clear-Seal for a small covered porch on a budget. Whatever you choose, most of the result comes from prep: clean, repair, let it dry, apply thin coats in mild weather, and write down what you used.
